title: Your neighbourhood
description: Say where you are from, and describe the place you live.
grammar: ser de + a place, and estar cerca
grammarNote: Where you are from is ser de: soy de Madrid. Where you are now is estar: estoy cerca.

explanation.summary: Spanish uses two different verbs for two different kinds of place. Ser de says where something comes from, and estar says where it is right now. Getting this the right way round is one of the first things a learner notices.

sections.heading: Where you are from
sections.body: Ser de + a place says where you come from: soy de Madrid, eres de Arabia. It does not change with estar, because being from somewhere is not a position, it is a fact. You can also say eres de + a city with no article: soy de Sevilla.

sections.heading: Where you are now
sections.body: Estar says where a thing or a person is at this moment: el banco está en la plaza, mi casa está cerca de la estación. Near and far are adjectives, not prepositions: está cerca, está lejos.

examples.es: El banco está en la plaza.
examples.en: The bench is in the square.

examples.es: El hospital está cerca de la estación.
examples.en: The hospital is near the station.

examples.es: Mi casa está en un barrio tranquilo.
examples.en: My house is in a quiet neighbourhood.

sections.heading: Describing a place
sections.body: A place is described with ser: el barrio es tranquilo, la plaza es grande. A thing is described with estar: el barrio está tranquilo today, la plaza está llena. Ser says what it is, estar says how it is right now.

examples.es: La plaza está llena de gente.
examples.en: The square is full of people.

items.note: Masculine: el barrio. It also means a district of a city.
Feminine: la plaza. It is the square in a town.
Masculine: el banco. It also means a bank.
Feminine: la fuente. It also means a source.
Masculine: el jardín. The accent marks the stress.

drills.meaning: the bench is in the square

drills.prompt: Mi casa está ___ de la estación.
drills.meaning: my house is near the station
drills.note: Near is an adjective, not a preposition.
What a place is uses ser.

drills.meaning: the square is full of people
drills.note: How a place is now uses estar.
